content: Palindromic rheumatism, also known as Hench-Rosenberg syndrome, is characterized by sudden and rapidly developing episodes of arthritis. These episodes are marked by acute pain, redness, swelling, and functional impairment of one or more joints, though typically only one joint is affected. The duration of these attacks and the intervals between them are highly variable. Importantly, no permanent joint damage occurs following these episodes. The exact cause of palindromic rheumatism remains unknown. However, it has been hypothesized to represent an abortive form of rheumatoid arthritis, as a significant proportion of patients exhibit anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies and antikeratin antibodies (AKA), which are also commonly found in rheumatoid arthritis. Palindromic rheumatism must be differentiated from other conditions such as acute gouty arthritis and atypical, acute-onset rheumatoid arthritis. Without specific diagnostic tests, such as joint fluid analysis, distinguishing palindromic rheumatism from other episodic joint disorders can be challenging. It is also important to recognize that individuals may have more than one autoimmune disorder simultaneously. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis and some other forms of arthritis, palindromic rheumatism affects men and women equally. It most commonly occurs in individuals between the ages of 20 and 50. The diagnosis of palindromic rheumatism is not confirmed by a single test. Instead, it is typically based on a thorough medical history and the presence of characteristic signs and symptoms. Due to the overlap of symptoms with other forms of arthritis and autoimmune diseases, diagnosis can be difficult and may take time. Often, other conditions must be ruled out before a definitive diagnosis is made, as there is no specific test for palindromic rheumatism. The term palindromic is derived from the word palindrome, which refers to something that reads the same forward and backward (e.g., kayak or mom). This reflects the nature of the disease, where episodes begin and end in a similar manner. Palindromic rheumatism is a rare form of inflammatory arthritis that causes sudden joint inflammation, typically involving one or several joints. These episodes last from a few hours to a few days and then resolve completely. The condition often affects two or three joints at a time, with symptoms developing over hours and lasting days to weeks before subsiding. Recurrence of episodes follows a pattern, with symptom-free intervals lasting weeks to months. Large joints are most commonly affected, and soft tissue involvement, such as swelling of periarticular tissues (e.g., heel pads and finger pads), is also observed. Subcutaneous nodules may occasionally be present. Systemic symptoms, such as fever, may or may not accompany joint swelling. On physical examination, laboratory findings are typically normal. Blood tests may reveal elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, but these findings are otherwise unremarkable. Rheumatoid factor may be present, particularly in individuals who are at higher risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis.
